summary: Defines how BGP can advertise IPv4 network layer reachability information using an IPv6 next hop. Previously the IPv4 address family definitions only allowed IPv4 next hops. It was later replaced by RFC 8950.

eli5.summary: A router can tell others about old-style addresses even when it is itself reached through the new style of address. This note makes that allowed. It was later replaced by RFC 8950.

subtitle: Advertise old-style addresses across a new-style network backbone.

tldr.problem: BGP routers can tell other routers about IPv4 network addresses, but the current rules force them to use an IPv4 address as the next hop, making it hard to operate IPv4 islands across an IPv6 backbone.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC extends BGP to allow an IPv6 address as the next hop for IPv4 routes, with a capability announcement so peers can agree they both support it.
tldr.outcome: Carriers can now run IPv4 networks across IPv6 transit cores without extra conversion layers. RFC 8950 later updated this specification.

today: RFC 5549 is Proposed Standard and specifies how BGP speakers can advertise IPv4 routes across IPv6 backbones using IPv6 next hops. It has been obsoleted by RFC 8950, which provides updated specifications.

sections.title: The Problem: IPv4 Over IPv6
sections.content:
RFC 4760 defines how Multiprotocol BGP (MP-BGP) advertises reachability. It uses an Address Family Identifier (AFI) and Subsequent Address Family Identifier (SAFI) to describe what kind of routes are being advertised and what kind of address can serve as the next hop. The current AFI/SAFI rules for IPv4 routes only allow IPv4 next hop addresses.

However, carriers and enterprises face situations where they operate IPv4 customer networks (islands) connected across an IPv6 backbone. The RFC cites two examples from the literature: IPv4 islands across an IPv6 core, and IPv6 islands across an IPv4 core. When using MP-BGP to advertise these routes, routers need to advertise IPv4 routes with an IPv6 next hop, which the current specification forbids.
sections.eli5: Imagine you need to mail a postcard about addresses in the old town (IPv4) but send it through the new transit center (IPv6). Right now the rules say you can only use old addresses for the directions, but you need to use new directions.

sections.title: Extending AFI/SAFI Definitions
sections.content:
This RFC extends the definition of AFI/SAFI pairs for IPv4 NLRI and VPN-IPv4 NLRI (AFI/SAFI <1/1>, <1/2>, <1/4>, and <1/128>). Instead of restricting next hops to IPv4 addresses, it allows next hops to be either IPv4 or IPv6.

The method for determining which address family the next hop belongs to uses the Length of Next Hop Address field. When this field is 4 octets, the next hop is IPv4. When it is 16 octets, the next hop is IPv6. This same technique is already used by RFC 4684 and L2VPN specifications.
sections.eli5: The solution is simple: look at how long the next hop address is. If it is short, it is the old style. If it is long, it is the new style.

sections.title: BGP Capability Advertisement
sections.content:
Routers cannot simply start sending IPv6 next hops without agreeing first. RFC 5492 defines a capability advertisement mechanism. This RFC defines a new capability called Extended Next Hop Encoding with capability code 5.

When a BGP speaker wants to advertise IPv4 or VPN-IPv4 NLRI with an IPv6 next hop, it first advertises this capability to its peer. The capability value field carries triples of (NLRI AFI, NLRI SAFI, Nexthop AFI). For this RFC, the relevant combination is NLRI AFI = 1 (IPv4), NLRI SAFI = 1/2/4/128, and Nexthop AFI = 2 (IPv6). A BGP speaker MUST only send such routes after confirming via capability advertisement that the peer supports them.
sections.eli5: Before sending the new-style directions, the two routers shake hands and agree they both understand how to handle them.

sections.title: Deployment Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives two usage scenarios. First, IPv4 over IPv6 Core: Address Family Border Routers (AFBRs) advertise IPv4 NLRI in the MP_REACH_NLRI along with an IPv6 Next Hop. The MP_REACH_NLRI uses AFI = 1, SAFI = 1, a Next Hop length of 16 or 32 octets containing an IPv6 address, and IPv4 routes as the NLRI.

Second, IPv4 VPN over IPv6 Core: PE routers advertise VPN-IPv4 NLRI in the MP_REACH_NLRI along with an IPv6 Next Hop. The structure is similar but with SAFI = 128 for VPN routes. During capability advertisement, these routers include Extended Next Hop Encoding with the appropriate AFI/SAFI/Nexthop combinations.
sections.eli5: The RFC shows two real situations: connecting old networks through a new backbone, and connecting old virtual networks through a new backbone.

sections.title: Operations and Status
sections.content:
By default, a BGP speaker should use an address of the same family as its own address when sending routes. This behavior can be overridden by policy. When a Route Reflector passes a route unchanged (as is normal), it MUST NOT change the next hop encoding. If a client cannot handle the encoding, the route cannot be distributed to that client.

RFC 5549 was published as Proposed Standard in May 2009 and defines the specification. However, it has been obsoleted by RFC 8950, which provides updated guidance on this functionality.
sections.eli5: Routers should normally use familiar addresses, but network operators can choose differently. Once set, an address type should not be changed in the middle. This RFC was later replaced by a newer version.
